pr.title: Encode `coroutine_by_move_body_def_id` in crate metadata
pr.description:
We synthesize the MIR for a by-move body for the `FnOnce` implementation of async closures. It can be accessed with the `coroutine_by_move_body_def_id` query. We weren't encoding this query in the metadata though, nor were we properly recording that synthetic MIR in `mir_keys`, so the `optimized_mir` wasn't getting encoded either!

Stacked on top is a fix to consider `DefKind::SyntheticCoroutineBody` to return true in several places I missed. Specifically, we should consider the def-kind in `fn DefKind::is_fn_like()`, since that's what we were using to make sure we ensure `query mir_inliner_callees` before the MIR gets stolen for the body. This led to some CI failures that were caught by miri but which I added a test for.
pr.author: compiler-errors

classification.name: Inline

The concrete pass affected is `Inline`. The patch makes synthetic by-move coroutine bodies available in `mir_keys` and changes the `cross_crate_inlinable` result for `SyntheticCoroutineBody`, which the `Inline` pass directly consults. Extending `DefKind::is_fn_like()` also ensures `mir_inliner_callees` is computed before MIR is stolen, fixing the `-Zinline-mir` regression exercised by the added test.

analysis.summary: Confirmed bug fix in the Inline-related compiler pipeline for async closures. The synthetic by-move MIR body of a coroutine-closure's FnOnce implementation was neither recorded in `mir_keys` nor encoded/decoded through a metadata table, and `DefKind::SyntheticCoroutineBody` was omitted from function-like/inlining classifications. Consequently `optimized_mir` was not encoded for that body and the Inline infrastructure failed to ensure `mir_inliner_callees` before MIR was stolen, causing a Steal ICE under `-Zinline-mir`; cross-crate inlining also could not recognize the synthetic body. The fix makes the synthetic def-kind fn-like, adds it to cross-crate inlinability and symbol-mangling global-sharing checks, encodes `coroutine_by_move_body_def_id` in metadata, and inserts the synthetic body into `mir_keys`.
analysis.originalLogic: `mir_keys` collected only `tcx.hir().body_owners()` plus tuple struct/variant constructors found by a `GatherCtors` HIR visitor, so the synthetic by-move MIR body of an async closure was absent. The metadata encoder recorded only `coroutine_for_closure` for coroutine-closures, and no `coroutine_by_move_body_def_id` table existed. `DefKind::is_fn_like()` returned true only for `DefKind::Fn | DefKind::AssocFn | DefKind::Closure`. `cross_crate_inlinable` returned true only for `DefKind::Ctor(..) | DefKind::Closure`, and symbol mangling treated only `DefKind::Fn | DefKind::AssocFn | DefKind::Closure | DefKind::Ctor(..)` as globally shared functions. The Inline pipeline therefore classified `SyntheticCoroutineBody` as non-function-like and could steal MIR without first ensuring `mir_inliner_callees`.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historically incorrect transformation is to treat a `DefKind::SyntheticCoroutineBody` produced for an async closure's `FnOnce` implementation as if it were not a function-like MIR body: omit it from `mir_keys`, fail to encode/decode `coroutine_by_move_body_def_id` in crate metadata, return false from `DefKind::is_fn_like()` and `cross_crate_inlinable`, and exclude it from the symbol-mangling globally-shared-function set. This loses the synthetic body's optimized MIR, prevents the inline pass from ensuring `mir_inliner_callees` before the MIR is stolen, and prevents valid cross-crate inlining. The corrected behavior includes the synthetic body in all those places and encodes the metadata query. A separate agent can contrast a program whose async closure is invoked so its by-move `FnOnce` body is needed (e.g. through `impl async FnOnce` or across a crate boundary) against the same program using a path that does not require the synthetic by-move body, then compile with `-Zinline-mir` and cross-crate metadata.
analysis.inputDomain: Rust programs using async closures (feature `async_closure`), especially calls that require the closure's by-move `FnOnce` coroutine body, with `-Zinline-mir` and/or an async closure exported and called from another crate. Relevant conditions include `tcx.needs_coroutine_by_move_body_def_id(coroutine_for_closure)` being true and metadata being encoded for the defining crate then decoded by a dependent crate.
analysis.trigger: An async closure is used in a context requiring its synthetic by-move body, such as calling it through `impl async FnOnce`, or when such a closure is defined in one crate and consumed in another. With `-Zinline-mir`, the Inline machinery may process the synthetic body without having ensured `mir_inliner_callees`, producing a Steal ICE; cross-crate optimization may also miss or mis-handle the body because its def-id is absent from metadata.
preconditions: `#![feature(async_closure)]` and an async closure whose `FnOnce` implementation needs a synthesized by-move body
The compiler must encode/decode crate metadata for `coroutine_by_move_body_def_id` when the defining and consuming crates differ
`-Zinline-mir` enables the inlining path that must ensure `mir_inliner_callees` before MIR is stolen
`mir_keys` must contain the synthetic body so its optimized MIR is produced and encoded
`DefKind::SyntheticCoroutineBody` must be recognized as function-like and cross-crate inlinable, and as a globally shared function for symbol mangling
pitfalls: Assuming every MIR body has an HIR `BodyId`: the synthetic by-move body must be added to `mir_keys` explicitly from `coroutine_by_move_body_def_id`.
Encoding only `coroutine_for_closure` but not `coroutine_by_move_body_def_id`, which leaves cross-crate consumers unable to find the synthetic body and leaves its optimized MIR unencoded.
Omitting `DefKind::SyntheticCoroutineBody` from `is_fn_like()`; this is the classification used to ensure `mir_inliner_callees` before the MIR is stolen, so omission can cause a Steal ICE.
Omitting `SyntheticCoroutineBody` from `cross_crate_inlinable`, preventing the Inline pass from treating the synthetic body like other closure bodies.
Omitting it from the symbol-mangling globally-shared-function match, risking symbol conflicts for synthetic coroutine bodies.
Replacing the constructor-collection visitor is a separate refactor; do not confuse constructor MIR collection with the async-closure metadata/Inlining defect.
analysis.testStrategy: Add a build-pass UI regression test using an async closure that is passed to an `async fn call_once<T>(f: impl async FnOnce() -> T) -> T { f().await }` and driven by a polling `block_on`, compiled with `-Zinline-mir`, to exercise the synthetic by-move body through Inline and catch the former Steal ICE. Also extend a cross-crate async-closure fixture so the foreign async closure is passed to a local `impl async FnOnce` consumer, exercising metadata encoding/decoding of `coroutine_by_move_body_def_id` and cross-crate inlinability. Check optimized MIR is available for the synthetic body, not merely that compilation succeeds. No compiler was built or executed here; these are source-backed testing recommendations.

-        matches!(self, DefKind::Fn | DefKind::AssocFn | DefKind::Closure)
+        matches!(
+            self,
+            DefKind::Fn | DefKind::AssocFn | DefKind::Closure | DefKind::SyntheticCoroutineBody
+        )

// If this async closure has a by-move body, record it too.

+    // body that isn't in the HIR.
